Recorded caught for that reason; alloc_arena names where the chain lives. Introduced in 1.3.9 with chunked encoding support per the commit message. Advisory severity: medium. Vulnerable 1.3.9-1.11.0.

trigger: ngx_walk_tree() freed ctx->data on exit whenever ctx->alloc was set, including on paths where THIS invocation had not allocated it -- so a nested walk could free the caller's buffer, and the caller would free it again. Found by a contributor
poc: Recursive directory walk (e.g. cache loader) where an inner ngx_walk_tree level takes the failure path without having allocated ctx->data
notes: CONTROL GROUP, and the oldest row here. Object: ctx->data = ngx_alloc(ctx->alloc, ctx->log) at src/core/ngx_file.c:970 -- real malloc, real ngx_free. The fix introduces a local `data` so only the allocation made by this invocation is freed. A textbook double free of a malloc chunk, i.e. the one bug class where glibc's own tcache/fastbin checks abort the process; the pool has no equivalent because ngx_pfree on a small object simply returns NGX_DECLINED and does nothing (ngx_palloc.c:277-294) -- a 'double free' there is silent by construction. Non-CVE; predates nginx's CVE practice.

trigger: If configuration parsing fails, ngx_regex_module_init() is never called and the global ngx_pcre_studies stays set, pointing into a pool that has already been freed. A later RUNTIME regex compilation (SSI, for instance) walks that list -- in single-process mode, or in a worker respawned from a master left in this state.
poc: A configuration that fails to parse, in single-process mode, followed by a runtime regex compilation via SSI
notes: Object: the ngx_pcre_studies ngx_list_t and its elements, allocated from the configuration cycle's pool. The fix clears the global from the pool CLEANUP handler, which is the arena-native answer: because the pool frees everything at once and ngx_pfree cannot free an individual element (ngx_palloc.c:277-294), the only hook available is a cleanup callback on the pool itself. Blind: the dangling global points at a block that has gone back to malloc, but everything that shared the block is indistinguishable, and while the cycle pool is alive the stale entries are simply live arena bytes. Related later fix: 25c546ac37ba622b93c1a7075bd7eb447bac17b2 (1.25.0) fixed a NULL deref in the same cleanup path when the studies list allocation itself failed. Non-CVE.

trigger: A body filter returns an error; ngx_event_pipe_drain_chains() returns ALL buffers to p->free_raw_bufs including those in p->busy, which the downstream still owns. If upstream EOF is seen in the same ngx_event_pipe() pass, those buffers are reused for new upstream reads while still queued for the client. With HTTP/2 only the stream's fake connection is marked on error, so ngx_http_v2_send_output_queue() keeps sending DATA frames pointing at them.
poc: Proxy with buffering to an HTTP/2 client, where an error occurs in the output filter chain while upstream EOF arrives in the same event-pipe pass
notes: Objects: the pipe's raw buffers, `ngx_create_temp_buf(p->pool, p->bufs.size)` at src/event/ngx_event_pipe.c:240, where p->bufs = u->conf->bufs (src/http/ngx_http_upstream.c:3495) = proxy_buffers, whose default is 8 buffers of ngx_pagesize (ngx_conf_merge_bufs_value(conf->upstream.bufs, prev->upstream.bufs, 8, ngx_pagesize) at src/http/modules/ngx_http_proxy_module.c:3750-3751) = 4096 on this host, one byte ABOVE pool->max=4095, so the data areas take ngx_palloc_large -> malloc; the ngx_buf_t headers (80 bytes) and the chain links (16 bytes) are bump carves. Verdict blind anyway, and this is the clearest reason why: the buffers are never free()d -- they are recycled through the pipe's OWN p->free_raw_bufs list (ngx_event_pipe.c:318-321, :379-380, :1083-1094) and the chain links through pool->chain (ngx_buf.c:48-65). The commit's own words are 'the pipe no longer treats a downstream it has given up on as merely blocked' and the fix is to leave p->busy intact so the buffers are freed only with the request pool. A malloc-level defence sees nothing because malloc is never told. Non-CVE; listed in CHANGES 1.31.5 as 'use-after-free might occur ... proxying with buffering ... HTTP/2 client'.

affected_function: ngx_http_upstream_copy_content_type (src/http/ngx_http_upstream.c:5645; the added guard is at :5682), consumed by ngx_http_header_filter
trigger: Upstream Content-Type of `charset="`. p and last both point just past the opening quote; the trailing-quote strip did `if (*(last - 1) == '"') last--;` without checking last > p, so last < p and `r->headers_out.charset.len = last - p` wraps to SIZE_MAX. ngx_http_header_filter then hands that to ngx_cpymem. ASAN verdict quoted in the fix commit: negative-size-param.
poc: an upstream response carrying multiple 103 status lines; two consecutive `Content-Type: ...charset="` headers trigger the ASAN report (described in the fix commit)
notes: WEAK BLIND - counted blind by the mechanical arena rule but honestly a poor example of it. Destination: `src/http/ngx_http_header_filter_module.c:442 b = ngx_create_temp_buf(r->pool, len);` -> `src/core/ngx_buf.c:22 b->start = ngx_palloc(pool, size);`, and a typical response header block is a few hundred bytes, well under r->pool->max (ngx_palloc.c:34 gives 4095 for the default 4k request_pool_size), so the buffer really is bump-carved. But the copy length is SIZE_MAX, so it escapes the memnode, the pool and every mapping: a page fault stops it regardless of allocator bounds, and ASAN's negative-size-param is a memcpy interceptor check that does not depend on arena membership at all. This is the ONLY nginx commit in the whole repository that references OSS-Fuzz (verified by `git log --all -i --grep=oss-fuzz`, with a --grep=pool positive control).

trigger: A rewritten URI containing a NUL byte. The path buffer is sized from r->uri.len but filled with ngx_cpystrn, which stops at the NUL, leaving the tail of the buffer holding whatever bytes were previously in that pool region; the full path->len was then used, exposing those bytes (e.g. through the Location header).
poc: Configuration that rewrites a URI containing an escaped %00, then returns a redirect whose Location is built from the mapped path
notes: Object: path.data from ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, path->len) at src/http/ngx_http_core_module.c:2000. ngx_pnalloc does NOT zero (only ngx_pcalloc does, ngx_palloc.c:297-308), and ngx_reset_pool (ngx_palloc.c:111-114) rewinds d.last without zeroing, so the uninitialised tail is literally the previous request's bytes from the same arena block. Size is root.len + uri.len + 1, normally well under 4095. This is the purest form of the arena problem: the disclosure is of NEIGHBOURING LIVE-THEN-RECYCLED arena content, and no allocator boundary is crossed at all, so no spatial or temporal allocator check could fire. Non-CVE (commit message describes the exposure; not in the CHANGES security list).

trigger: A request terminated by ngx_http_terminate_request() while an AIO operation is running in a SUBREQUEST. The finalizer was only installed on the subrequest where terminate was called, not on the one running the AIO, so normal processing resumed there after completion -- against an upstream connection that the termination had already closed.
poc: Cache background update with aio threads, where the client closes the connection during the update (ticket #2555)
notes: Objects: the subrequest ngx_http_request_t (ngx_pcalloc(r->pool, sizeof(ngx_http_request_t)), 1336 bytes measured, src/http/ngx_http_core_module.c:2452) and the upstream ngx_connection_t (per-worker array, ngx_alloc at src/event/ngx_event.c:754-755, recycled via free_connections). Observed symptoms in the commit are 'segfaults in ngx_ssl_recv(), readv() failed (9: Bad file descriptor) ... or socket leaks' -- the classic signature of a recycled slot rather than a freed chunk. Blind on both objects: the subrequest is a carve inside the main request's live pool, and the connection slot is never returned to malloc. Ticket #2555. Non-CVE.

trigger: Copying ngx_http_variable_value_t structures into the geo binary base copies the uninitialised 'escape' field and the struct's padding holes; a crc32 is then computed over that data. Found with MemorySanitizer.
poc: A geo{} block with a binary base (geo $var { ranges; ... }) built at configuration time; MSan reports the crc32 over uninitialised bytes
notes: Object: val = ngx_palloc(ctx->pool, sizeof(ngx_http_variable_value_t)) at src/http/modules/ngx_http_geo_module.c:1262 (identical bug in src/stream/ngx_stream_geo_module.c:1212). sizeof measured at 16 bytes -- as small as a pool object gets, so unambiguously the bump path. The fix is literally s/ngx_palloc/ngx_pcalloc/, which is the canonical arena remedy: because ngx_palloc never zeroes, EVERY struct allocated with it inherits the previous tenant's bytes in its padding. Non-CVE, config-time, low severity, but it is the cleanest possible demonstration of the mechanism, and it took MSan to find it because no allocator can.

trigger: When connecting to a backend, if the read event handler ran before the write event handler and the received response triggered a next-upstream condition, ngx_http_upstream_reinit() was never called. With ngx_http_grpc_module and ngx_http_proxy_v2_module, ctx->connection was then left pointing at an object allocated from the PREVIOUS upstream connection's pool, which had been destroyed -- and it was reused for the next upstream.
poc: grpc_pass or proxy_pass (HTTP/2) to a backend that sends a next-upstream-triggering response immediately, with proxy_next_upstream enabled
notes: Object: the shared gRPC/HTTP2 connection object hung off the peer connection's pool cleanup and cached in ctx->connection (src/http/modules/ngx_http_grpc_module.c:4393 and :4420, cleared at :1341); the module context itself is ngx_pcalloc(r->pool, sizeof(ngx_http_grpc_ctx_t)) at :575. The freed memory belongs to the upstream connection pool, which ngx_destroy_pool does return to malloc (ngx_palloc.c:89-95) -- but the surviving pointer is an interior pointer into that block, and the same commit records the non-memory-safety half (mixed responses, duplicate headers) which no allocator addresses at all. Fix adds u->response_received so reinit runs. CHANGES 1.29.5: 'use-after-free might occur after switching to the next gRPC or HTTP/2 backend'. A companion commit a29476464cc86092135401bdcad91e4d38ac6b6d resets ctx->out/in/busy on gRPC reinit. Non-CVE.

trigger: Truncated upstream response with no Content-Length. ctx->length is then the ALLOCATION size (image_filter_buffer), not the number of bytes actually received, and the size parser and image decoders treated it as the amount of valid data -- parsing and decoding past the received bytes into uninitialised buffer memory.
poc: Upstream that omits Content-Length and closes the connection mid-image, through a location using image_filter
notes: Object: ctx->image = ngx_palloc(r->pool, ctx->length) at src/http/modules/ngx_http_image_filter_module.c:482. The size expression is the crux: at :274 ctx->length = conf->buffer_size (image_filter_buffer, default 1M) when Content-Length is absent -- far above pool->max=4095, hence ngx_palloc_large -> malloc; at :277 ctx->length = the response's Content-Length, which for a small image can be BELOW 4095 and then becomes a bump carve. So the same object changes arena depending on the response, and the buggy path (no Content-Length) is precisely the large/malloc one. Marked caught per the control-group rule, with the caveat that the over-read stays INSIDE the single malloc'd allocation, so bounds checking would not fire either -- only initialisation tracking (MSan-style) would. The one-line fix sets ctx->length = p - ctx->image once the body is read. Non-CVE.

trigger: Same class as CVE-2026-42533 but on the access-log line: the log format's length pass and copy pass could disagree (variables with side effects, or values that grow between passes), and the copy ops had no end check.
poc: Any access_log format whose variables can change value between nginx's length and copy passes (e.g. a volatile map variable), on a request that triggers logging
notes: Object: the log line buffer, allocated `line = ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, len)` at src/http/modules/ngx_http_log_module.c:370, where len is the sum of the format's per-op length callbacks. Typical access-log lines are a few hundred bytes, so this is the bump path; it exceeds 4095 only with unusually large logged values. 185 lines changed in the http log module plus 101 in the stream one, all adding room checks. Non-CVE (shipped with the 1.31.3 script-hardening set but not itself named in the advisory). Blind for the same reason as the script row: adjacent pool objects, no boundary.

trigger: Request URI shorter than the location prefix, which happens after try_files replaces the URI. loc_len was set to plcf->location.len unconditionally, so r->uri.data + loc_len points past the URI and (r->uri.len - loc_len) underflows to a huge size_t, which ngx_escape_uri then walks.
poc: location /1234 { try_files /123 =404; proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080/; } requested as '/123'
notes: Object: r->uri.data. After try_files the URI is a fresh small ngx_pnalloc from r->pool; before any rewrite it points into the request header buffer, which is either the 1k client_header_buffer (pool, bump path) or an 8k large_client_header_buffer (malloc). The overread length is ~2^64 so it runs off the end of the arena block and eventually segfaults -- but the FIRST several kilobytes it reads and escapes into the upstream request are neighbouring pool objects belonging to the same request, i.e. a disclosure window that no arena boundary marks. Fixed by ngx_min(plcf->location.len, r->uri.len). Non-CVE; GitHub issue #983. Verdict blind for the bytes that matter (the adjacent ones); a guard page eventually stops the walk, which is why this presented as a segfault rather than a quiet leak.

trigger: Standalone 'break' directive used in a location where the URI had been rewritten, together with 'alias' or a proxy_pass with a URI component. Same shape as the proxy bug: location prefix longer than the rewritten URI.
poc: location /aaa/ { rewrite ^ /xxx/yyy; break; proxy_pass http://localhost:8080/bbb/; }
notes: Object: the rewritten r->uri.data, an ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, e->buf.len) carve from ngx_http_script.c:1232, tens of bytes -> bump path. The commit says explicitly 'if location's prefix was longer than the rewritten URI, a segmentation fault might occur'. Recorded as a separate row from the 2025 proxy fix because it is the SAME defect class in the same family six years earlier, which is the kind of recurrence this survey is meant to surface. Non-CVE. Blind: the read starts inside the pool block and walks forward over neighbours.

trigger: A script result shorter than its predicted length. The predicted length allocates the buffer, the copy pass writes fewer bytes, and the string was still returned with the PREDICTED length, so the tail was uninitialised pool bytes sent to the client.
poc: map $uri $foo { ~^/(?<bar>[0-9]).*$ $bar; } location ~(?<bar>[0-9]*)[a-z]*$ { return 200 $1:$foo; } requested as '/1234abcd'
notes: Object: e->buf.data from ngx_pnalloc(e->request->pool, len) at src/http/ngx_http_script.c:1861 (and the rewrite module's own copy). Variable-sized, essentially always < 4095 -> bump path. The leaked bytes are the previous occupant of that arena region within the same request pool, or of a reset pool (ngx_reset_pool, ngx_palloc.c:111-114, does not zero). Non-CVE: it shipped in 1.31.3 alongside CVE-2026-60005 but is a separate commit and is not itself in the CHANGES security list. Verdict blind: the read never leaves the allocation, so even a perfectly bounds-checked allocator sees nothing wrong -- only initialisation tracking would.

trigger: An SSI command whose parameter name is exactly NGX_HTTP_SSI_PARAM_LEN (32) bytes long and is followed by '-'. The error branch appended the '-' to the key without re-checking key.len, writing key.data[32].
poc: SSI-processed response containing `<!--# include <32-byte-param-name>- -->`
notes: Object: ctx->param->key.data, allocated ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, NGX_HTTP_SSI_PARAM_LEN) at src/http/modules/ngx_http_ssi_filter_module.c:1245-1246. Size is the compile-time constant 32, always far below pool->max=4095, so it is always a bump-pointer carve. The 1-byte overwrite at index 32 lands on whatever ngx_palloc handed out next in the same pool block (the very next allocation in ngx_http_ssi_parse is ctx->param->value.data at :1256). nginx pool: ngx_palloc_small is a pure bump pointer (ngx_palloc.c:156-167), no header/size/free bit; ngx_pfree walks only pool->large (ngx_palloc.c:277-294) so it is a no-op on a small pool object; pool->max measured at 4095 on this 4K-page host. No allocator sees the write: there is no redzone, no size field and no chunk boundary between the 32-byte key and its neighbour. Non-CVE.

trigger: Filter finalization while working with an upstream: error_page redirects to a simple handler, ngx_http_request_finalize() terminates the request via the upstream cleanup handler and closes the upstream socket -- while ngx_event_pipe() is still on the stack. The error was not noticed until control returned, so the pipe read from the already-closed socket.
poc: location /t2 { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080/big; } with a filter that finalizes (e.g. image_filter error) and error_page redirecting to a static handler
notes: Object: the upstream ngx_connection_t, from the per-worker array `cycle->connections = ngx_alloc(...)` at src/event/ngx_event.c:754-755, recycled through cycle->free_connections (ngx_connection.c:1229-1239 / :1279-1280) with ngx_memzero on reuse. The commit reports 'readv() failed (9: Bad file descriptor) ... or even segfaults with SSL'. Verdict blind despite the malloc arena, for the reason stated on the QUIC post-close row: ngx_free_connection never calls free(), so no allocator-level temporal check can fire; the slot is simply handed to a different connection. The SSL segfault comes from the c->ssl object, which is ngx_pcalloc'd from the connection pool. Non-CVE.

trigger: Unbuffered request-body reading not finished before the request is redirected by error_page or X-Accel-Redirect, and the body is then read again: duplicate post_handler call, or 'http request count is zero' alert followed by a segmentation fault.
poc: location / { proxy_request_buffering off; proxy_pass http://bad; proxy_intercept_errors on; error_page 502 = /error; } over HTTP/2 with a request body still arriving
notes: Object: ngx_http_request_t (1336 bytes measured) from `ngx_pcalloc(pool, sizeof(ngx_http_request_t))` at src/http/ngx_http_request.c:589, out of the request_pool_size pool created at :584 (default 4k, giving pool->max = 4016). 'http request count is zero' is nginx's own name for a reference-count underflow, i.e. a premature free of the request and its pool -- and the DATA frames still being processed by the HTTP/2 connection then write into it. Blind: r->request_body, the body buffers and the request itself are all carves from the same pool block, so nothing distinguishes a live one from a freed one until the whole block goes back to malloc. Ticket #1819. Non-CVE. The fix skips DATA frames while r->reading_body is set without no-buffering.

trigger: 400 errors redirected to an upstream server with error_page. The request never finished header processing, so r->request_body is NULL, but DATA frames from the client were still fed to the body machinery.
poc: error_page 400 = /upstream; location /upstream { proxy_pass http://backend; } then send an HTTP/2 request with a malformed header block followed by DATA frames
notes: Object: r->request_body (ngx_http_request_body_t), normally ngx_pcalloc'd from r->pool; here never allocated at all, so the dereference is of NULL rather than of arena memory. Recorded as a pool row because that is where the object would have lived and because the surrounding request state is all arena, but the honest note is that a NULL dereference is caught by the MMU on every allocator, so the arena is not what makes this one dangerous -- it is included for completeness of the HTTP/2 body-handling family alongside the 1.17.4 row above, which IS arena-dependent. The bug was introduced in 1.13.0 and the fix mirrors an earlier one in the same file. Non-CVE. || VERDICT NORMALISED BY THIS SESSION: counted 'caught' because a NULL dereference is trapped by page protection on any hardware, independent of the allocator. It is NOT evidence that the arena is visible to CHERI, and it is NOT evidence of blindness either; it is excluded from the blind count on purpose so the headline figure stays conservative. alloc_arena still records the true origin of the object.

trigger: The response-header length accumulator started at 0 but the encoder always emits a 2-byte QPACK field-section prefix, so the buffer was allocated two bytes short of what was written into it.
poc: Any HTTP/3 response (the two prefix bytes are unconditional)
notes: Object: b = ngx_create_temp_buf(r->pool, len) -- at the buggy revision, src/http/v3/ngx_http_v3_request.c:368, with the under-computed len set at :266. Response header blocks are hundreds of bytes, so this is a bump carve and the 2-byte overflow lands squarely on the next pool object. The fix is literally `len = 0;` -> `len = 2;`. Fixed on the pre-release HTTP/3 branch so it never shipped as a defect, but it is the archetype: a hand-maintained length prediction, a separate write pass, and an arena with no boundary to catch the disagreement -- the same shape as CVE-2026-9256 and CVE-2026-42945 six years later. Non-CVE.

trigger: An empty header value sent in a literal header representation. On that path st->value.data was never assigned at all, so it still held the pointer left over from the PREVIOUS header parsed on the same connection. Consumers, which expect a NUL-terminated value, then read from that stale pool address.
poc: HTTP/3 request containing a header field with a zero-length literal value
notes: Object: st->value.data. On the normal path it points at a pool carve: `st->last = ngx_pnalloc(c->pool, n + 1)` at src/http/v3/ngx_http_v3_parse.c:649, assigned to st->value.data at :655 -- a per-header-value bump allocation, essentially always well under pool->max=4095. On the zero-length-literal path the assignment was simply skipped, leaving the field pointing at the previous header value's buffer in the same connection pool. The one-line fix assigns a static empty string (the same guard now appears at :833, :956 and :1097). Blind: the stale pointer is a perfectly valid, in-bounds pointer into a live arena block, so nothing about it is detectable -- and because the pool never zeroes (ngx_palloc.c:156-167) and never individually frees (:277-294), the bytes it names are real, attacker-influenced content from earlier in the same request. Fixed on the pre-release HTTP/3 branch. Non-CVE.

trigger: Per RFC 9204 3.2.2 a new QPACK dynamic-table entry may reference an entry that will be evicted by that same insertion. nginx evicted BEFORE inserting, so the insertion read the name out of the entry it had just freed. Insert-with-Name-Reference and Duplicate encoder instructions.
poc: HTTP/3 encoder stream sending an Insert With Name Reference (or Duplicate) whose referenced entry is the one the insertion will evict
notes: CONTROL GROUP, and a direct in-module comparison with CVE-2026-42530 above. Object: ngx_http_v3_field_t, allocated `ngx_alloc(sizeof(ngx_http_v3_field_t) + name->len + value->len, c->log)` at src/http/v3/ngx_http_v3_table.c:246 and released with a real `ngx_free(field)` at :397 (the entry array likewise ngx_alloc at :337 / ngx_free at :344, :372). So the QPACK dynamic table deliberately sits on malloc rather than the connection pool -- entries outlive individual streams and must be individually freeable, which the pool cannot do (ngx_pfree is a no-op on small pool objects, ngx_palloc.c:277-294). That makes this UAF a genuine caught case: free() is called, and the reuse is exactly what a quarantining allocator detects. Ticket #2431. The fix evicts after inserting. Non-CVE.

trigger: A TLSv1.3 session whose session id exceeds 32 bytes -- legal under TLSv1.3, where session ids are arbitrary and delivered as session tickets. The cache node has a fixed 32-byte id array, so the copy runs past it into the rest of the slab node and beyond.
notes: No CVE assigned; included as the survey's ngx-slab data point. ALLOC SITE READ: src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c:4430 `sess_id = ngx_slab_alloc_locked(shpool, n);` with n = sizeof(ngx_ssl_sess_id_t) on LP64 (:4424-4425), and the overflowing copy at :4465 `ngx_memcpy(sess_id->id, session_id, session_id_length);`. The target is `u_char id[32]` at src/event/ngx_event_openssl.h:171, and the very next member is `u_char *session` (:173) -- the pointer that :4464 then writes THROUGH, so an oversized session id corrupts a pointer and the following memcpy dereferences it. SLAB VERDICT REASONING: blind. ngx_slab_free_locked only flips bookkeeping bits inside a zone that is mmap'd once at ngx_cycle.c and released only on configuration reload; nothing per-object ever reaches the system allocator, so CHERI performs no revocation and no re-bounding and a stale or overrunning pointer stays a valid in-bounds capability into the live zone. The one difference from the nginx pool worth recording is instrumentability, not detection: slab at least HAS a per-object free CALL SITE that a hooking allocator could instrument, whereas the pool has none for small objects. The fix simply refuses to cache sessions with an id longer than 32 bytes.

trigger: `ssl_ocsp` configured; a client SSL connection is terminated (typically by timeout) while the OCSP responder name is still being resolved. The OCSP context was freed but the resolver context was not, so the DNS completion callback dereferenced resolve->data.
poc: ssl_ocsp on; with a slow/unresponsive DNS resolver, and a client that disconnects during the handshake
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/event/ngx_event_openssl_stapling.c:1312 `ctx = ngx_pcalloc(pool, sizeof(ngx_ssl_ocsp_ctx_t));` out of a dedicated pool created one line earlier at :1307 `pool = ngx_create_pool(2048, log);` (pool->max = 2048-80 = 1968, so the ctx is a bump allocation). The dangling pointer is resolve->data, set at :1436 and dereferenced in ngx_ssl_ocsp_resolve_handler. The fix stores ctx->resolve and calls ngx_resolve_name_done() from ngx_ssl_ocsp_done() at :1345-1347. HONEST CAVEAT ON THE VERDICT: unlike the SSI subrequest case, this ctx's pool IS destroyed (ngx_destroy_pool(ctx->pool) at :1353) and ngx_destroy_pool DOES ngx_free the whole block chain (ngx_palloc.c:89-95), so a revoking allocator would see the 2 KB block die. Recorded blind per the arena rule; what remains genuinely invisible is object granularity -- every pointer into that 2 KB block, to any of the objects sharing it, is equally stale and equally unbounded. The resolver context on the other side of this bug is malloc'd (see CVE-2021-23017 notes). Vulnerable 1.19.0-1.30.0. || ARENA VERIFIED BY THIS SESSION, OVERRIDING ANY OTHER CLASSIFICATION: the whole nginx resolver subsystem is on SYSTEM MALLOC, not the pool. ngx_resolver_alloc is a thin wrapper over ngx_alloc (= malloc) at src/core/ngx_resolver.c:4161; ngx_resolver_calloc calls it and memzeroes (:4170-4181); ngx_resolver_free is a real ngx_free (= free) at :4189, as is ngx_resolver_free_locked (:4198). So resolver objects get a real per-object bounds event on allocation and a real revocation event on free -- CHERI sees them. This makes nginx's most famous memory-safety CVEs CONTROL GROUP rows, not blind-spot rows, which is a substantive result rather than a bookkeeping detail. || Object: ngx_ssl_ocsp_ctx_t, 456 bytes, ngx_pcalloc from its dedicated 2048-byte pool at src/event/ngx_event_openssl_stapling.c:1307-1312 (pool->max there = 1968). The fix adds a ctx->resolve back-pointer so ngx_ssl_ocsp_done() can call ngx_resolve_name_done(). Note the asymmetry this row captures: the resolver's OWN ngx_resolver_ctx_t is real malloc (ngx_resolver_alloc -> ngx_alloc, src/core/ngx_resolver.c:4161, 224 bytes measured) and would be caught, while the OCSP ctx it points back at is arena memory and is not. Same bug, two allocators, two different detectabilities. Advisory text confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.31.0. Second use-after-free in this file after the 2020 one above, in the same error-teardown area.

trigger: A response decoded from UTF-8 via charset_map where one multi-byte UTF-8 character is split across 3 or more single-byte buffers. ngx_utf8_decode() was called with the last saved-array INDEX instead of the byte COUNT, and the following ngx_memcpy() used the same index as a length, reading past the input buffer.
poc: Upstream response with a 3-byte UTF-8 sequence delivered one byte per buffer, through a location with charset/charset_map converting from utf-8
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: same objects as CVE-2026-48142 -- the input buffer is the upstream response buffer from src/event/ngx_event_pipe.c:240 ngx_create_temp_buf(p->pool, p->bufs.size) or src/http/ngx_http_upstream.c:2483 ngx_palloc(r->pool, u->conf->buffer_size), both 4096 by default and therefore ngx_palloc_large = real malloc (threshold 4016). The pre-fix loop is visible in the diff at ngx_http_charset_filter_module.c:785-792 and the bad copy at the old :826. Same intra-object caveat as CVE-2026-48142: the paired write into `u_char saved[4]` (declared at ngx_http_charset_filter_module.c:73, inside the ngx_pcalloc'd ctx at :404) stays within the ctx allocation and is invisible to any bounds checker. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. Advisory severity: low. Vulnerable 0.3.50-1.30.0. CVE-2026-48142 is the follow-up 1-byte case in the same function. || Two objects. (a) Destination: ctx->saved, a 4-byte array (NGX_UTF_LEN=4, ngx_http_charset_filter_module.c:18) embedded in ngx_http_charset_ctx_t, which is allocated ngx_pcalloc(r->pool, sizeof(ngx_http_charset_ctx_t)) at :404 and :519; sizeof measured at 72 bytes, always a bump carve. ngx_memcpy(&ctx->saved[ctx->saved_len], src, i) with saved_len+i > 4 writes into the neighbouring fields of the very same 72-byte pool object. (b) Source: the response buffer being recoded, which for proxied responses is u->buffer (ngx_palloc(r->pool, u->conf->buffer_size) at ngx_http_upstream.c:2483, default 4k/8k -> usually the large/malloc path). Verdict blind on the object that decides it: the write side never leaves the 72-byte pool struct, so it is invisible to ANY allocator, malloc or arena. Advisory text confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.31.0.

trigger: A response body decoded from UTF-8 via charset_map, where an INVALID multi-byte UTF-8 sequence is split across buffer boundaries. ngx_utf8_decode() stops advancing at the first invalid byte, so the saved-sequence pointer is left short and one extra byte is consumed from the next buffer.
poc: Upstream response containing a deliberately invalid multi-byte UTF-8 sequence split across buffers, through charset_map from utf-8
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: the over-read object is the upstream response body buffer `buf` whose bytes are consumed at src/http/modules/ngx_http_charset_filter_module.c:785-786. With proxy_buffering on (default) those buffers come from src/event/ngx_event_pipe.c:240 `b = ngx_create_temp_buf(p->pool, p->bufs.size);` with proxy_buffers default 8 x ngx_pagesize = 4096 (ngx_http_proxy_module.c:3750-3751); the first one is u->buffer from src/http/ngx_http_upstream.c:2483 `u->buffer.start = ngx_palloc(r->pool, u->conf->buffer_size);` with proxy_buffer_size also ngx_pagesize. 4096 > the 4016 request-pool threshold, so both are ngx_palloc_large = real malloc, and a 1-byte read past a full buffer is a bounds violation a CHERI-bounded pointer traps on. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. NUANCE WORTH RECORDING: the companion write `ngx_memcpy(&ctx->saved[ctx->saved_len], src, len)` targets `u_char saved[NGX_UTF_LEN=4]` at ngx_http_charset_filter_module.c:73, a member of ngx_http_charset_ctx_t allocated by ngx_pcalloc(r->pool, sizeof(ngx_http_charset_ctx_t)) at :404. In the pre-fix code that write could reach saved[5], i.e. 2 bytes past the array but still INSIDE the same allocation (the next members are the `length:16`/`from_utf8:1` bitfields). An intra-object overflow like that is invisible to CHERI and to every allocator, arena or not. Advisory severity: low. Vulnerable 0.3.50-1.31.1. || Same object as CVE-2026-42934: ctx->saved[4] inside the 72-byte ngx_http_charset_ctx_t from ngx_pcalloc(r->pool, ...) at ngx_http_charset_filter_module.c:404/:519. The fix clamps `saved` up to &ctx->saved[ctx->saved_len]. A 1-byte overread that stays inside the same pool object -- structurally undetectable by an allocator, and it is the SECOND fix in the same three-line region in two months, which is the pattern worth recording. Advisory text confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.31.2.

component: nginx/ngx_http_core_module (try_files in a regex location with alias)
trigger: A long URI handled by try_files inside a regex location that also uses alias. The reserve was computed as ngx_abs((ssize_t)(len - r->uri.len)) + alias + 16, which under-reserves for a regex alias location, so building the candidate filename overflows the path buffer. nginx ticket #135.
notes: No CVE was assigned; recorded because it is the same allocation and the same failure mode as CVE-2026-27654 fourteen years earlier. ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_core_module.c:2000 `path->data = ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, path->len);` inside ngx_http_map_uri_to_path(), reached from ngx_http_core_try_files_phase() with the under-computed `reserve`. The fix splits the reserve calculation into three cases (no alias / regex location with alias / plain alias) and tracks `allocated` separately. SIZE: a filesystem path, a bump allocation under the 4016 threshold. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432.

trigger: DAV COPY or MOVE in a location with `alias`, where the Destination URI is SHORTER than the alias prefix. `r->uri.len - alias` underflows size_t, the wrapped sum yields a small path->len, and the following copy writes far past it.
poc: COPY/MOVE request with Destination shorter than the configured alias, against a location { alias /some/long/path/; dav_methods COPY MOVE; }
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_core_module.c:2000 `path->data = ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, path->len);` where path->len = clcf->root.len + reserved + r->uri.len - alias + 1 (two lines above). The overwrite happens in the trailing `last = ngx_copy(last, r->uri.data + alias, r->uri.len - alias);` of the same function. SIZE: a filesystem path, well under 4016, so a bump allocation; the neighbours it corrupts are other per-request pool objects, which is exactly why the commit message says the practical effect is 'a change of the source or destination file names to be outside of the location root' rather than a crash. That is the signature symptom of an intra-arena overflow: the process keeps running with silently corrupted adjacent data. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. The fix rejects duri.len < clcf->alias in ngx_http_dav_copy_move_handler. Related earlier hardening: f0a084645 (1.31.0, 'Dav: improved path validation for COPY and MOVE operations'). Vulnerable 0.5.13-1.29.6. || Object: path.data, allocated ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, path->len) at src/http/ngx_http_core_module.c:2000, with the underflowing length computed one line earlier at :1998. Size expression root.len + reserved + uri.len - alias + 1; the attacker chooses the wrapped result, and the interesting case is precisely the one where it wraps back BELOW 4095, i.e. into the bump-allocated small path. The commit message states the overwrite 'could result in a change of the source or destination file names to be outside of the location root' -- i.e. the corrupted neighbour is another pool object. nginx pool: ngx_palloc_small is a pure bump pointer (ngx_palloc.c:156-167), no header/size/free bit; ngx_pfree walks only pool->large (ngx_palloc.c:277-294) so it is a no-op on a small pool object; pool->max measured at 4095 on this 4K-page host. Advisory text confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.29.7. Also carries a CVE; recorded here because it was found through the commit history.

affected_function: ngx_http_mp4_read_stsc_atom / read_stts_atom / read_stss_atom / read_ctts_atom / read_stsz_atom / read_stco_atom / read_co64_atom
trigger: A crafted mp4 whose atom entry count makes the pointer expression `atom_table + entries * sizeof(entry)` overflow, so the 'atom too large' test is bypassed and the update passes index entries far outside the atom, overwriting memory in the worker.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/modules/ngx_http_mp4_module.c:887 (release-1.1.18) `mp4->buffer = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, mp4->buffer_size);` with mp4_buffer_size defaulting to 512 * 1024 at :2861 -- ngx_palloc_large = real malloc. The fix (208 insertions) replaces the overflow-prone `atom_end = atom_table + entries * sizeof(...)` pointer comparison with arithmetic on ngx_mp4_atom_data_size() in every reader, introduces the ngx_mp4_atom_data_size() macro, and reworks ngx_http_mp4_read() to take a required size. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. Advisory severity: major, 'potentially resulting in arbitrary code execution'. Vulnerable 1.1.3-1.1.18 and 1.0.7-1.0.14. This is the commit whose release (1.1.19) becomes the lower bound of the 2026 mp4 advisories.

trigger: A crafted mp4 with a 64-bit atom whose declared size is 0 or smaller than the 64-bit atom header. Subtracting the header size underflows the atom data size, giving a CPU hog or an enormous read length.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/modules/ngx_http_mp4_module.c:1083 `mp4->buffer = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, mp4->buffer_size);`, mp4_buffer_size default 512 KB (:3983) so ngx_palloc_large = real malloc. The fix adds `if (atom_size < sizeof(ngx_mp4_atom_header64_t))` right after the 64-bit size is read. The commit message states the consequences directly: 'CPU hog when the size is 0, or various other problems due to integer underflow when calculating atom data size, including segmentation fault or worker process memory disclosure'. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. Advisory: memory disclosure, severity medium. Vulnerable 1.1.3-1.15.5 and 1.0.7-1.0.15.

affected_function: ngx_http_mp4_read_ftyp_atom / read_moov_atom / read_mdat_atom / read_mvhd_atom / read_tkhd_atom / read_mdia_atom (and the rest)
trigger: A crafted mp4 containing a DUPLICATE atom in a container. The module re-ran the reader for the second copy, overwriting trak->out[] entries and the cached atom buffers that earlier passes had already sized and populated, so later update passes wrote using stale sizes.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/modules/ngx_http_mp4_module.c:1083 `mp4->buffer = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, mp4->buffer_size);` (default 512 KB, so ngx_palloc_large = real malloc), which is where the atom tables that get mis-sized live. SECOND ALLOC SITE READ, and it points the other way: :1138 `ftyp_atom = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, atom_size);` in ngx_http_mp4_read_ftyp_atom, where atom_size = 8 + atom_data_size and the function rejects atom_data_size > 1024 -- so the ftyp copy is at most 1032 bytes and IS a pool bump allocation. This CVE therefore straddles both arenas: corruption inside mp4->buffer is caught, corruption of the small per-atom pool copies is blind. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. One commit fixes both CVE-2022-41741 and CVE-2022-41742; its message says 'worker process crash, memory corruption and disclosure'. The fix adds a duplicate check to every atom reader. Vulnerable 1.1.3-1.23.1 and 1.0.7-1.0.15.

affected_function: ngx_http_mp4_read_ftyp_atom / read_moov_atom / read_mdat_atom / read_mvhd_atom / read_tkhd_atom (and the rest)
trigger: Same crafted duplicate-atom mp4 as CVE-2022-41741; this is the disclosure half, where the mismatched atom state causes the module to emit bytes from outside the intended atom region into the response.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/modules/ngx_http_mp4_module.c:1083 `mp4->buffer = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, mp4->buffer_size);`, mp4_buffer_size default 512*1024 (:3983), so always ngx_palloc_large = real malloc. Same single fix commit as CVE-2022-41741 -- nginx assigned two CVEs (memory corruption and memory disclosure) to one 147-line change that adds duplicate-atom rejection to every reader. Recorded as two rows because the advisory does. Caveat carried over from CVE-2024-7347: because every atom table is a REGION INSIDE one 512 KB malloc'd buffer rather than its own allocation, a disclosure that stays within that buffer is not a bounds violation and would not trap; only reads leaving the 512 KB block would. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. Vulnerable 1.1.3-1.23.1 and 1.0.7-1.0.15.

trigger: A crafted mp4 where (next_chunk - chunk) * samples overflows 32 bits in ngx_http_mp4_crop_stsc_data(), producing a huge trak->end_chunk_samples, which ngx_http_mp4_update_stsz_atom() then turns into a read before the start of the stsz atom.
poc: mp4 file with an stsc atom whose chunk-run times samples-per-chunk exceeds 2^32, served through mp4; and requested with a start offset
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/modules/ngx_http_mp4_module.c:1083 `mp4->buffer = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, mp4->buffer_size);` -- the stsz atom data is a region inside that one buffer, default 512 KB, hence ngx_palloc_large = real malloc. The commit message describes it as 'reading memory before stsz atom start', i.e. a backwards underread; because the atom sits INSIDE the mp4 buffer rather than being its own allocation, a small underread stays inside the malloc'd block and would NOT trap -- only an underread large enough to leave the 512 KB block does. Worth flagging as a limitation of bounds checking against a coarse-grained buffer. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. Fix widens n to uint64_t; companion 88955b1044ef38315b77ad1a509d63631a790a0f rejects unordered stsc chunks, which otherwise made trak->end_chunk < trak->start_chunk and overread in ngx_http_mp4_update_stco_atom(). Advisory severity: low. Vulnerable 1.5.13-1.27.0. || Object: mp4->buffer = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, mp4->buffer_size) at src/http/modules/ngx_http_mp4_module.c:1083; buffer_size is mp4_buffer_size, default 512K (:3983), so ngx_palloc_large -> malloc. Two size caveats that matter for this survey: (a) at :1072-1073 buffer_size is shrunk to (mp4->end - mp4->offset) for a short file, so a small enough mp4 makes this a POOL object; (b) at :1243 it is set to NGX_HTTP_MP4_MOOV_BUFFER_EXCESS = 4096 (:1172), one byte over pool->max, so that path stays malloc. The containing ngx_http_mp4_file_t is itself 6960 bytes (measured) from ngx_pcalloc(r->pool, ...) at :617, hence also large/malloc. Marked caught: the read goes BEFORE the buffer start, which a malloc-level bounds check does see. Fix widens n to uint64_t. Advisory: worker process crash. This is the control-group counterpart to the pool rows -- the same class of arithmetic bug, but landing in an allocator that has boundaries.

trigger: A crafted mp4 that produces zero-size output buffers, in particular empty stco and co64 atoms, and a start/end time selection with no data between them. The code clamped end_offset to start_offset and carried on, producing buffer overread and overwrite.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: same object as CVE-2026-27784 -- src/http/modules/ngx_http_mp4_module.c:1083 `mp4->buffer = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, mp4->buffer_size);`, default 512 KB, always a `large` allocation = real malloc. The atom tables (stco/co64/stsc/stsz entries) are pointers INTO that one buffer, not separate objects, so both the overread and the overwrite are bounds violations of a single malloc'd block and a CHERI-bounded pointer traps. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. The fix turns `if (end_offset < start_offset) end_offset = start_offset;` into a hard error at ngx_http_mp4_module.c:901-907. Companion in the same release: 18a70a4d5 (1.31.1, 'Mp4: avoid adding or comparing to null pointer'). Vulnerable 1.1.19-1.29.6.

affected_function: ngx_http_mp4_read_stts_atom / stss / ctts / stsc / stsz / stco / co64
trigger: A crafted mp4 whose atom entry count multiplied by the entry size overflows 32-bit size_t, so the 'atom too small' validation passes and the module then indexes entries beyond the atom, reading and writing outside the allocated mp4 buffer.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/modules/ngx_http_mp4_module.c:1083 `mp4->buffer = ngx_palloc(mp4->request->pool, mp4->buffer_size);` in ngx_http_mp4_read(). CONTROL-GROUP ROW: mp4_buffer_size defaults to 512*1024 (ngx_http_mp4_module.c:3983) and mp4_max_buffer_size to 10 MB (:3984-3985), so this is always ngx_palloc_large = real malloc with real bounds; the commit message itself says 'reads and writes outside of the allocated mp4 buffer'. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. The fix casts entries to uint64_t in all seven validation expressions. EDGE CASE: ngx_http_mp4_read() clamps buffer_size to the remaining file length at :1072-1073, so for an mp4 file smaller than ~4 KB the same buffer would become a pool bump allocation and the same bug would be blind. Advisory: 32-bit platforms only. Vulnerable 1.1.19-1.29.6. Distinguished from the sibling CVE-2026-32647 by the repo's own changes.xml, which tags this one 'on 32-bit platforms'.

trigger: A crafted request URI containing '/../' sequences. The handler did `u -= 4;` and then scanned BACKWARDS with `while (*(u - 1) != '/') u--;`, checking the lower bound only once before the scan, so the loop could walk below the start of the URI buffer.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_request.c:723 (release-0.8.14) `r->uri.data = ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, r->uri.len + 1);` -- allocated only when r->complex_uri or r->quoted_uri is set, which is exactly the path this bug is on. SIZE: the request URI, bounded by client_header_buffer_size (1k default) or large_client_header_buffers (8k), so for ordinary requests a bump allocation under the 4016 threshold. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. The fix moves the bound check INSIDE the loop: `u -= 5; for(;;) { if (u < r->uri.data) return NGX_HTTP_PARSE_INVALID_REQUEST; if (*u == '/') { u++; break; } u--; }`. A backwards walk out of a bump-allocated object is the hardest case for an arena: it runs into whatever this request allocated EARLIER, which under a pool is guaranteed to be live, attacker-influenced request state. Advisory title 'Buffer underflow vulnerability', severity major. Vulnerable 0.1.0-0.8.14.

trigger: A request header line beginning with CR followed by another character ('\rX'), with error_log at info or debug level. r->header_name_start was never assigned on that path, so the logging call formatted from a NULL pointer.
notes: One-line fix: `r->header_name_start = p;` added to the CR case in src/http/ngx_http_parse.c:746. ALLOC SITE READ for the buffer the pointer should have addressed: r->header_in, ngx_create_temp_buf(r->pool, cscf->client_header_buffer_size) with the 1k default -- a request-pool bump allocation. VERDICT REASONING, not following the arena rule: the fault is a NULL dereference in the log formatter, which traps on CHERI and on a conventional MMU alike, so caught regardless of arena. Worth contrasting with the pool rows: had the field held STALE pool bytes rather than NULL (ngx_pcalloc zeroes the request struct, which is the only reason it is NULL and not garbage) this would have been an unbounded read of recycled arena memory and entirely blind. Advisory title 'Null pointer dereference vulnerability', severity major. Vulnerable 0.1.0-0.8.13.

trigger: A chunked Transfer-Encoding request with a chunk size large enough to make ctx->size go negative. r->headers_in.content_length_n becomes negative, ngx_min() against the buffer size returns the negative value, and the size_t cast turns it into a huge recv() length into a 4096-byte on-stack array.
notes: READ THE SITE: src/http/ngx_http_request_body.c:630 (release-1.4.0) `u_char buffer[NGX_HTTP_DISCARD_BUFFER_SIZE];` -- a STACK array, not a heap object at all; NGX_HTTP_DISCARD_BUFFER_SIZE is 4096 (src/http/ngx_http_request.h:19). The overflowing call is :649-652 `size = (size_t) ngx_min(r->headers_in.content_length_n, NGX_HTTP_DISCARD_BUFFER_SIZE); n = r->connection->recv(r->connection, buffer, size);`. ARENA FIELD CAVEAT: recorded as system-malloc because the enum has no 'stack' value -- it is NOT malloc'd. The verdict still holds for the right reason: under pure-capability CHERI a stack array carries exact bounds like any other allocation, so the smash traps. The four-line fix is `if (ctx->size < 0 || ctx->length < 0) goto invalid;` in ngx_http_parse_chunked(). The identical change was committed on three branches: this one on 1.4.1, 818807d71 on 1.5.0 and 2265b3c2b on 1.2.9. Introduced in 1.3.9 per the changelog. Advisory severity: major, 'potentially resulting in arbitrary code execution'.

component: nginx/ngx_http_proxy / fastcgi / scgi / uwsgi header processing
trigger: A backend response header containing an embedded NUL byte. ngx_cpystrn() stops at the NUL, so fewer bytes are written than h->key.len / h->value.len claim, and the untouched tail of the freshly bumped buffer -- never zeroed by ngx_pnalloc -- is then sent to the client.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/modules/ngx_http_proxy_module.c:1375-1376 (at the fix commit) `h->key.data = ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, h->key.len + 1 + h->value.len + 1 + h->key.len);` with h->value.data and h->lowcase_key carved out of the same block. TEXTBOOK BLIND ROW, and the closest historical analogue to CVE-2026-60005: ngx_pnalloc does not zero (only ngx_pcalloc does, ngx_palloc.c:297-308), the pool never scrubs on reset (ngx_reset_pool just rewinds d.last, ngx_palloc.c:111-114), and small pool objects are never individually freed (ngx_pfree walks only pool->large and returns NGX_DECLINED, ngx_palloc.c:277-294). The changelog wording is exactly the arena signature: 'content of previously freed memory might be sent to a client'. SIZE: a header key plus value, tens to hundreds of bytes, far under the 4016 threshold. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. The fix replaces each ngx_cpystrn() with an explicit ngx_memcpy() of the known length plus a manual NUL. Advisory severity: major. Vulnerable 0.1.0-1.1.16.

trigger: proxy_pass to an untrusted HTTP backend that returns a malformed chunked response. The same negative ctx->chunked.size as CVE-2013-2028 makes `buf->last - buf->pos >= ctx->chunked.size` trivially true and `buf->pos += ctx->chunked.size` move the cursor BACKWARDS below the start of the upstream buffer, so the resulting output buffer spans memory the response never filled.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: with proxy_buffering on the body buffers come from src/event/ngx_event_pipe.c:240 `b = ngx_create_temp_buf(p->pool, p->bufs.size);` with proxy_buffers defaulting to 8 x ngx_pagesize = 4096 each (src/http/modules/ngx_http_proxy_module.c:3750-3751), and the first response buffer from src/http/ngx_http_upstream.c:2483 `u->buffer.start = ngx_palloc(r->pool, u->conf->buffer_size);` with proxy_buffer_size also ngx_pagesize. 4096 exceeds the 4016 request-pool threshold, so both are ngx_palloc_large = real malloc and a cursor pushed below b->start is a bounds violation. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. SAME FIX COMMIT as CVE-2013-2028 -- one four-line guard in ngx_http_parse_chunked() covers both the client-request and the upstream-response paths; MITRE describes this one as being in ngx_http_proxy_module.c and 'a similar vulnerability to CVE-2013-2028'. Recorded as its own row because the advisory lists it separately with a different affected range (1.1.4-1.2.8 and 1.3.9-1.4.0) and a different consequence (memory disclosure rather than stack smash).

trigger: `ignore_invalid_headers off;` plus a very large `large_client_header_buffers`, then a crafted request proxied to an HTTP/2 or gRPC backend. A header field longer than NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_FIELD needs more HPACK integer octets than the NGX_HTTP_V2_INT_OCTETS=4 the length pass budgeted for, so the write pass runs past the frame buffer.
poc: ignore_invalid_headers off; large_client_header_buffers 4 64k; grpc_pass/proxy_pass to an HTTP/2 backend; then send a request with a very long URI or method
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/modules/ngx_http_grpc_module.c:944 `b = ngx_create_temp_buf(r->pool, len);` (and src/http/modules/ngx_http_proxy_v2_module.c:602 for proxy_v2), where len is the computed HTTP/2 HEADERS frame size. CONTROL-GROUP ROW. NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_FIELD = 127 + (1 << 21) - 1 = 2097278 (src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.h:24-25), so reaching the bug at all requires a header field over ~2 MB, which forces len far above the 4016-byte request-pool threshold. ngx_palloc therefore takes the ngx_palloc_large path (ngx_palloc.c:220) = a genuine ngx_alloc/malloc with real bounds, so a CHERI-bounded allocator traps on the overflowing store. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. The fix adds explicit NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_FIELD rejections for method, URI, :authority and every header name/value; see also 58a7bc3406ac (1.31.1) and 44c66e92c (1.31.3) for the response-side counterparts. || Object: the upstream request buffer, b = ngx_create_temp_buf(r->pool, len) at src/http/modules/ngx_http_grpc_module.c:944 (mirrored in ngx_http_proxy_v2_module.c). Size expression: a sum of 1 + NGX_HTTP_V2_INT_OCTETS + field.len over every header. For a normal request that total is a few hundred bytes -- a bump carve, and the overflow lands on neighbouring request-pool objects. The configuration named in the advisory (large_client_header_buffers with LARGE values) is what pushes the fields big enough to break the 4-octet assumption; it can also push len over 4095 into the malloc path, but the encoding overflow is present at both sizes. Fix rejects fields above NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_FIELD before allocating, and a follow-up (44c66e92c88bf2367dd31efc9d5843c0838d11f2, 1.31.3) applies the same limits to RESPONSE header parsing. Advisory text confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.31.2.

trigger: A Range header whose individual ranges sum past NGX_MAX_OFF_T_VALUE, defeating the total-size restriction and, via a suffix range such as `bytes=-100` on a short resource, producing a range with a NEGATIVE start.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: the range list is ctx->ranges, an ngx_array_t initialised against r->pool in ngx_http_range_parse's caller, and the negative start it holds is consumed as a FILE offset. IMPORTANT SCOPE NOTE, and the reason this row's verdict should not be read as a CHERI claim: the out-of-bounds access here is not a memory access at all. The bad value flows into pread() and sendfile() offsets ('pread() ... failed (22: Invalid argument)' in the commit message) and, when proxy_cache is used, lets the client read the cache FILE HEADER that precedes the cached body. No pointer leaves any allocation, so neither CHERI bounds nor revocation are engaged in either direction; recorded blind only because the containing objects are pool-allocated. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. Companion d289616b0fb452f7dd4cbb4534c706950e3d6c24 stops suffix ranges producing a negative start at all. Advisory: 'sensitive information leak', severity medium. Vulnerable 0.5.6-1.13.2.

trigger: A `rewrite` whose replacement string contains arguments (e.g. `rewrite ^(.*) /new?c=1;`) followed by a `set` or `if` that evaluates a capture. e->is_args was set and never cleared, so escaping was applied to later captures whose buffer had been sized without escaping.
poc: location / { rewrite ^(.*) /new?c=1; set $myvar $1; return 200 $myvar; }
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_script.c:1861 `e->buf.data = ngx_pnalloc(e->request->pool, len);` in ngx_http_script_complex_value_code(), where len is summed by the length codes at :1856-1858 with le.is_args copied from the engine -- the stale is_args made the WRITE pass escape while the LENGTH pass had not. The one-line fix is `e->is_args = 0;` at ngx_http_script.c:1205. SIZE: a variable value, tens of bytes; bump allocation. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. The commit notes an identical earlier bug fixed in 74d939974d43. Vulnerable 0.6.27-1.30.0. || Object: e->buf.data from ngx_pnalloc(e->request->pool, len) at src/http/ngx_http_script.c:1861, where len came from the length pass that did not account for escaping. Escaping is 3x expansion per escaped byte, so the overrun is many bytes, not one. Sizes here are variable-value sized, normally tens to hundreds of bytes -> always the bump path. nginx pool: ngx_palloc_small is a pure bump pointer (ngx_palloc.c:156-167), no header/size/free bit; ngx_pfree walks only pool->large (ngx_palloc.c:277-294) so it is a no-op on a small pool object; pool->max measured at 4095 on this 4K-page host. The commit notes a similar issue was fixed before in 74d939974d43, i.e. this class recurs in the same function family. Advisory text confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.31.0.

trigger: A `rewrite` whose replacement has no variables but OVERLAPPING captures, together with the `redirect` parameter or arguments in the replacement (e.g. `rewrite ^/((.*))$ http://127.0.0.1:8080/$1$2 redirect;` with URI `/++++...`). The escape budget was computed once over r->uri instead of per capture, so the buffer is shorter than the string written into it.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_script.c:1232 `e->buf.data = ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, e->buf.len);` -- e->buf.len is accumulated at :1225-1230 from code->size plus per-capture lengths plus the ngx_escape_uri budget the fix moved inside the capture loop. trigger: A backend response whose first line is not a recognisable status line, split across reads. The scgi/uwsgi fallback re-entered header parsing with a stale r->state and a buffer position past the bytes already consumed, so the header parser walked off the end of the upstream buffer.

notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_upstream.c:2483 `u->buffer.start = ngx_palloc(r->pool, u->conf->buffer_size);` with u->buffer.end set at :2492. CONTROL-GROUP ROW, but only just: scgi_buffer_size / uwsgi_buffer_size default to ngx_pagesize (ngx_http_scgi_module.c:1481-1483, ngx_http_uwsgi_module.c:1746-1748) = 4096, which is 80 bytes over the request pool's 4016 threshold, so ngx_palloc takes the ngx_palloc_large path = real malloc with real bounds and the overread traps. Configure `scgi_buffer_size 2k;` and the SAME BUG becomes a blind intra-pool overread -- a good illustration that the verdict here is a property of one config constant, not of the code. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. Advisory severity: medium. Vulnerable 0.8.42-1.30.0. || Object: u->buffer, allocated `u->buffer.start = ngx_palloc(r->pool, u->conf->buffer_size)` at src/http/ngx_http_upstream.c:2483; buffer_size is scgi_buffer_size / uwsgi_buffer_size, whose default is exactly ngx_pagesize (src/http/modules/ngx_http_scgi_module.c:1481-1483; the uwsgi module matches) = 4096 on this host. That is ONE byte above pool->max = 4095, so the default lands on ngx_palloc_large -> malloc by the narrowest possible margin. Marked caught on that basis, with the caveat that an operator who sets scgi_buffer_size to 4k-or-less-by-one, or runs on a platform with a larger page size for the pool cap, moves this object into the bump arena and loses the boundary entirely. The two-line fix is `r->state = 0;` in each module; a companion commit 5f86648ef8c969e98aa2f7b938472296b12055be adds `u->buffer.pos = status->line_start` backtracking for status lines split across reads. trigger: A map variable with regex matching used in a string expression AFTER a capture affected by that map (or any non-cacheable variable in a string expression). The length pass and the copy pass disagree, so the copy writes more bytes than were reserved.
poc: map $uri $map { ~(?<capture>.*) $capture; } set $capture ""; set $temp "$capture $map";
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_script.c:87 `value->data = ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, len);` in ngx_http_complex_value(), where len is the total computed by the length codes. The fix adds an e->end pointer plus ngx_http_script_check_length() (new function at ngx_http_script.c:820-836) to every copy code. It could exceed 4016 (and so become a real malloc) only with a URI approaching large_client_header_buffers (default 8k). pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. The overrun object is again e->buf.data from ngx_pnalloc(r->pool, len) at ngx_http_script.c:1232 / :1861. Advisory text (map + capture + string expression) confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.31.3.

trigger: A crafted SPDY request that leaves more than 2 * NGX_SPDY_STATE_BUFFER_SIZE bytes of unparsed state. sc->buffer_used then exceeds the headroom that ngx_http_spdy_read_handler() reserved, so the following recv() writes past the end of the shared SPDY receive buffer.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_spdy.c:401 (release-1.5.11) `smcf->recv_buffer = ngx_palloc(ngx_cycle->pool, smcf->recv_buffer_size);` with spdy_recv_buffer_size defaulting to 256 * 1024 (ngx_http_spdy_module.c:255). The cycle pool's max is 4095, so 256 KB is ngx_palloc_large = real malloc -- a control-group row. The overflowing write is `n = c->recv(c, end, available);` where `available = smcf->recv_buffer_size - 2 * NGX_SPDY_STATE_BUFFER_SIZE` and `end = p + sc->buffer_used`. THE FIX IS A ONE-CHARACTER CHANGE FROM `#if (NGX_DEBUG)` TO `#if 1` around the existing overflow check in ngx_http_spdy_state_save() -- i.e. the guard existed all along and was compiled out of production builds, which is worth noting for a survey about what checking buys you. NGX_SPDY_STATE_BUFFER_SIZE is 16 (ngx_http_spdy.h:23) and sc->buffer is a 16-byte member of ngx_http_spdy_connection_t (ngx_http_spdy.h:90), itself ngx_pcalloc(c->pool, ...) at ngx_http_spdy.c:410. Advisory severity: major, 'potentially resulting in arbitrary code execution'. Vulnerable 1.3.15-1.4.6 and 1.5.x before 1.5.12.

trigger: A crafted SPDY request whose 32-bit name or value length makes `r->header_name_end = p + len` wrap around the address space, so the `r->header_name_end > end` bounds test passes and the parser walks far past the header buffer.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_spdy.c:2261-2262 (release-1.5.10) `r->header_in = ngx_create_temp_buf(r->pool, cscf->client_header_buffer_size);` -- client_header_buffer_size defaults to 1k, comfortably under the 4016-byte request-pool threshold, so the SPDY header buffer the parser overruns IS a bump allocation with no header and no redzone. pool->max = min(pool_size - sizeof(ngx_pool_t), ngx_pagesize-1) at ngx_palloc.c:33-34; sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80 on LP64, so the REQUEST pool (request_pool_size default 4096, ngx_http_request.c:584) bumps anything <= 4016 and mallocs above that, and the CONNECTION pool (connection_pool_size default 64*sizeof(void*)=512, ngx_event_accept.c:159) bumps only <= 432. (If the header block is later moved to a large buffer at :2513 `ngx_create_temp_buf(r->pool, cscf->large_client_header_buffers.size)` with the 8k default, that copy would be a real malloc and the same overread would trap -- so the verdict depends on which buffer the request is parsed out of.) The fix replaces the wrap-prone pointer arithmetic with a remaining-length counter in r->lowcase_index and compares `(ngx_uint_t) (end - p) < r->lowcase_index`. Introduced in 1.5.10 per the changelog, which is why only that one release is vulnerable; companion 3925c1b11 ('SPDY: constant number of preallocated structures for headers'). Advisory severity: major, 32-bit platforms only.

trigger: A crafted proxied backend response with SSI includes during unbuffered proxying. A subrequest created for an SSI include while another include has data postponed gets posted twice (once by ngx_http_subrequest(), once by ngx_http_postpone_filter()), is finalized twice, over-decrements r->main->count and the request is torn down while still referenced.
poc: SSI page with two include statements, proxied with proxy_buffering off, where the second include's subrequest finalizes quickly while the first has postponed data
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_core_module.c:2452 `sr = ngx_pcalloc(r->pool, sizeof(ngx_http_request_t));` -- the subrequest is carved out of the PARENT request's pool and has no pool of its own (sr->ctx at :2462, its header lists at :2467/:2474 likewise). That is what makes this row strongly blind rather than merely arena-allocated: when the subrequest is 'freed' nothing is freed at all -- no ngx_free, not even a pool destroy -- the parent pool outlives it and the bytes stay valid and unchanged. A CHERI capability to the stale subrequest remains a perfectly in-bounds, unrevoked capability. The fix also allocates the ngx_http_posted_request_t at ngx_http_request.c:2660 from r->pool. sizeof(ngx_http_request_t) is a fixed compile-time size below the 4016 request-pool threshold (nginx's own request_pool_size default of 4096 is chosen so the request object itself is a bump allocation). Vulnerable 0.8.11-1.31.2. || Objects: the subrequest ngx_http_request_t, `sr = ngx_pcalloc(r->pool, sizeof(ngx_http_request_t))` at src/http/ngx_http_core_module.c:2452 -- sizeof measured at 1336 bytes, safely below pool->max, so a bump carve out of the PARENT request's pool -- and the ngx_http_posted_request_t link at :2481. The main request is `r = ngx_pcalloc(pool, sizeof(ngx_http_request_t))` at src/http/ngx_http_request.c:589 from a request_pool_size pool created at :584. Blind: the subrequest lives inside the main request's arena, so a premature ngx_http_free_request leaves every subrequest pointer aimed at bytes that are immediately reused for the next request through that pool -- and ngx_pfree on any of it is a documented no-op (ngx_palloc.c:277-294). The fix stops double-posting and, as hardening, resets r->write_event_handler to a no-op during finalization. Advisory text confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.31.3.

trigger: Unnamed regex captures combined with the `slice` directive or a background cache update. A volatile map with a non-matching regex reallocates r->captures in a subrequest without resetting r->ncaptures, so a later $1 read walks capture slots that were never written.
poc: map test $my_map { volatile; ~mismatch(.*) 1; default ""; } server { location ~(.*) { slice 50; ... } } -- the map reallocates r->captures in subrequests while the location regex set r->ncaptures
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/http/ngx_http_variables.c:2690 `r->captures = ngx_palloc(r->pool, len * sizeof(int));` with len = cmcf->ncaptures. The one-line fix is `r->ncaptures = 0;` at :2688. This is the cleanest 'blind' row in the survey: ngx_palloc does NOT zero (only ngx_pcalloc does, ngx_palloc.c:297-308), so the freshly bumped capture array carries whatever bytes the pool block held before. SIZE: (ncaptures+1)*3*sizeof(int) -- order of 100 bytes, far under 4016, so a bump allocation. A quarantining/zeroing malloc would blunt this; a bump allocator cannot. Disclosure of worker memory or worker termination. Vulnerable 1.15.8-1.31.2. || Object: r->captures, allocated `ngx_palloc(r->pool, len * sizeof(int))` at src/http/ngx_http_variables.c:2687 where len = cmcf->ncaptures = (max capture count + 1) * 3. For any realistic regex that is well under 4095 bytes, so it is a bump carve; it would need >340 capture groups to become a large/malloc block. ngx_palloc does not zero, so the stale offsets read are literally the previous occupant of that arena region -- and they are then used as string offsets into r->captures_data, which the advisory describes as 'worker process memory disclosure or worker process termination'. The one-line fix is r->ncaptures = 0. Textbook arena bug: uninitialised bytes with attacker-influenced prior content, invisible to any allocator. Advisory text confirmed in the fetched CHANGES under 1.31.3.

trigger: CRAM-MD5 or APOP authentication with authentication retry enabled. After the first attempt the code cleared s->passwd.data but left s->passwd.len non-zero, so the next attempt copied len bytes from a NULL pointer.
notes: The one-line fix replaces `s->passwd.data = NULL;` with `ngx_str_null(&s->passwd);` at src/mail/ngx_mail_auth_http_module.c:1331. ALLOC SITE READ for the containing object: src/mail/ngx_mail_handler.c:124 `s = ngx_pcalloc(c->pool, sizeof(ngx_mail_session_t));` -- a connection-pool bump allocation (connection pool->max = 432). VERDICT REASONING, and note it does NOT follow the arena rule: there is no allocated object being accessed out of bounds here. A NULL pointer is an untagged/invalid capability, so the dereference traps on CHERI exactly as it does on a conventional MMU, independently of which arena the session came from. Recorded as caught for that reason, with alloc_arena naming where the struct holding the NULL field lives. Companion hardening in the same release: 765642b86e0df1b5ef37f42522be7d08d95909c9 ('Mail: improved error handling in plain/login/cram-md5 auth methods'), which stops login/passwd being left half-set after a base64 decode error. Advisory severity: low. Vulnerable 0.5.15-1.29.6.
