trigger: A crafted UDP DNS response taking the format-error path. The resend-queue loop used `||` instead of `&&`, so iteration continued past the queue sentinel and treated non-node memory as an ngx_resolver_node_t.
notes: One-character fix: `q != ngx_queue_sentinel(&r->name_resend_queue) || times++ < 100` becomes `&&` in src/core/ngx_resolver.c. ALLOC SITE READ: the object misinterpreted is the queue SENTINEL, which is an ngx_queue_t embedded in the resolver itself -- src/core/ngx_resolver.c:142 `r = ngx_pcalloc(cf->pool, sizeof(ngx_resolver_t));` (configuration pool, NGX_DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE 16384 so pool->max = 4095; sizeof(ngx_resolver_t) is a few hundred bytes, hence a bump allocation). ngx_queue_data() subtracts offsetof(ngx_resolver_node_t, queue) from the sentinel address and the code then reads rn->... fields, i.e. it reads neighbouring ngx_resolver_t bytes as though they were a node and follows whatever pointers it finds -- the classic arena type confusion, and invisible because the read stays inside a live, long-lived pool block. Note the contrast with the OTHER resolver rows here (CVE-2021-23017, CVE-2016-0746, CVE-2011-4315), whose objects come from ngx_resolver_alloc = malloc: the resolver keeps its per-name state off the pool but the resolver STRUCT itself on it, and that is what decides the verdict. Debian's tracker maps this CVE to this commit. Advisory title: 'Invalid pointer dereference in resolver'. Vulnerable 0.6.18-1.9.9. || ARENA VERIFIED BY THIS SESSION, OVERRIDING ANY OTHER CLASSIFICATION: the whole nginx resolver subsystem is on SYSTEM MALLOC, not the pool. ngx_resolver_alloc is a thin wrapper over ngx_alloc (= malloc) at src/core/ngx_resolver.c:4161; ngx_resolver_calloc calls it and memzeroes (:4170-4181); ngx_resolver_free is a real ngx_free (= free) at :4189, as is ngx_resolver_free_locked (:4198). So resolver objects get a real per-object bounds event on allocation and a real revocation event on free -- CHERI sees them. This makes nginx's most famous memory-safety CVEs CONTROL GROUP rows, not blind-spot rows, which is a substantive result rather than a bookkeeping detail.

trigger: A crafted DNS response chain in which CNAME processing rewrote ctx->name to point at rn->u.cname, so a later lookup used a name buffer belonging to a resolver node that had since been freed. The paired timeout-handler bug stored the resolver NODE in ctx->event->data, which was then dereferenced after the node was freed.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: every object involved is malloc'd, not pooled -- src/core/ngx_resolver.c:810 and :1044 `rn = ngx_resolver_alloc(r, sizeof(ngx_resolver_node_t));`, :422 `ctx = ngx_resolver_calloc(r, sizeof(ngx_resolver_ctx_t));`, rn->name via ngx_resolver_dup (:4203-4216), and all of them released through ngx_resolver_free = ngx_free (:4185-4192). ngx_resolver_alloc is ngx_alloc = malloc at :4155-4166. CONTROL-GROUP ROW: real bounds, real free, so revocation fires on the stale ctx->name.data and on ev->data. The fix passes the CNAME as a separate ngx_str_t argument instead of overwriting ctx->name, and records ctx->node so ngx_resolve_name_done() no longer has to look the node up again. Debian's tracker maps this CVE to TWO commits: this one and 4b581a7c21e4328d059bf400a059c0458fc9f806 ('Resolver: fixed crashes in timeout handler', which changes ctx->event->data from rn to ctx and moves ident onto the ctx). Advisory severity: medium. Vulnerable 0.6.18-1.8.0 and 1.9.x before 1.9.10.

trigger: A DNS response larger than 255 bytes, where a compression pointer's first byte is 0xc1 or higher. The copy loop tested `n != 0xc0` and so treated the pointer byte as a literal label length, copying up to 255 bytes past the buffer the length pass had sized.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/core/ngx_resolver.c:1945 (release-1.1.7) `dst = ngx_resolver_alloc(r, len);` and the buggy loop immediately below at :1954-1960 `if (n != 0xc0) { ngx_memcpy(dst, src, n); dst += n; ... }`. ngx_resolver_alloc is ngx_alloc = malloc (ngx_resolver.c:4155-4166 in current sources), so this is a control-group row: a large overwrite of a malloc'd buffer with real bounds. The fix changes the test to `if (n & 0xc0)` and moves the pointer branch first, which is the same shape the function still has today. Same function and same allocation as CVE-2021-23017 ten years later -- two independent memory-safety bugs in one 40-line DNS name decoder, both landing on malloc rather than the pool. Advisory severity: medium. Vulnerable 0.6.18-1.1.7.

trigger: A forged UDP DNS response whose name encoding makes the copy loop emit one more '.' separator than the length pass counted, writing a single byte past the end of the name buffer. Requires the `resolver` directive and the ability to spoof packets from the configured DNS server.
notes: ALLOC SITE READ: src/core/ngx_resolver.c:4043 `dst = ngx_resolver_alloc(r, len);` in ngx_resolver_copy(). THE WHOLE RESOLVER IS A CONTROL GROUP: ngx_resolver_alloc is `ngx_alloc(size, r->log)` at ngx_resolver.c:4155-4166 and ngx_resolver_free is `ngx_free(p)` at :4185-4192 -- nginx deliberately keeps resolver state OFF the pool because it outlives any one request. So every resolver object has real malloc bounds and a real free, and a 1-byte overwrite past a malloc'd buffer is precisely the case a CHERI-bounded pointer traps on. This is the single most useful comparison point in the survey: the most famous nginx memory-safety bug is in the one subsystem that does not use the pool. The fix moves the '.' emission to the START of each label so the count matches the length pass; companion 077a890a76fff4f071776184aed881b5f314c98a fixes the off-by-one READ of the compression-pointer low byte in the same function (adds the `p >= last` check now at :4005-4008), which the commit calls harmless but which is an uninitialized read of the DNS response buffer. Advisory: 1-byte overwrite, potential arbitrary code execution. Vulnerable 0.6.18-1.20.0.

trigger: An SRV record that names the same host twice, combined with an allocation failure while reporting a subrequest result. The SRV resolve handler ran immediately with NGX_ERROR and freed the resolve context via ngx_resolve_name_done(), then the duplicate name reported again and used it.
notes: No CVE assigned. ALLOC SITE READ: the freed-and-reused object is an ngx_resolver_ctx_t from src/core/ngx_resolver.c:422 `ctx = ngx_resolver_calloc(r, sizeof(ngx_resolver_ctx_t));`, and ngx_resolver_calloc/alloc are ngx_alloc = malloc (:4155-4181) freed by ngx_resolver_free = ngx_free (:4185-4192). Control-group row: real bounds and a real free, so revocation fires. Included because it completes the resolver picture -- FOUR separate memory-safety defects (CVE-2011-4315, CVE-2016-0746, this one, CVE-2021-23017) in the one nginx subsystem that deliberately allocates off the pool, every one of them a case a conventional hardened allocator would catch. The fix routes both allocation-failure paths through a shared `done:` label so the handler runs only once all subrequests have completed.

trigger: A QUIC stream destroyed by its own read-event handler while inside ngx_quic_stream_input(). The stream-existence re-check read f->stream_id out of the frame struct -- but that frame had already been freed to the per-connection free list and reused (and partly zeroed) by the cleanup handler, so the check tested stream id 0.
poc: QUIC STREAM frame whose delivery causes the application handler to destroy the stream, while a stream with id 0x0 still exists
notes: Object: ngx_quic_frame_t, allocated `ngx_palloc(c->pool, sizeof(ngx_quic_frame_t))` at src/event/quic/ngx_event_quic_frames.c:218 and thereafter recycled entirely inside the arena: ngx_quic_alloc_frame pops from qc->free_frames (:205-207) and ngx_quic_free_frame pushes back (:252). This is the single best example in nginx of the free-list-inside-the-arena pattern flagged in the brief: the frame is 'freed' and handed to a DIFFERENT consumer with no allocator involvement whatsoever, and the stale read of frame->u.stream.stream_id returns another frame's contents. The fix copies the id out before calling the handler. Fixed on the pre-release QUIC branch, so it never shipped as a defect -- recorded because the mechanism is exactly the target class. Non-CVE.

trigger: ngx_quic_close_connection() does not always merely schedule a close timer -- if a close was already in progress it really closes the connection. Several callers kept touching the connection object afterwards. Additionally ngx_quic_stream_cleanup_handler() passed the STREAM connection instead of the QUIC connection, so streams were freed without shutting down their application contexts, producing a second use-after-free.
poc: QUIC session driven into a close path that is re-entered (e.g. an error during an already-started close)
notes: Object: ngx_connection_t. This is the one case where 'system-malloc' does NOT mean caught, and the source says so: the connection objects live in a single array allocated once per worker, `cycle->connections = ngx_alloc(sizeof(ngx_connection_t) * cycle->connection_n, ...)` at src/event/ngx_event.c:754-755, and are recycled through the cycle->free_connections singly-linked list (built at ngx_event.c:799, popped at src/core/ngx_connection.c:1229-1239, pushed back at :1279-1280) with an ngx_memzero on reuse. The array is never freed while the worker lives, so free() is never called and no allocator-level temporal check can fire; a stale ngx_connection_t* stays in-bounds of a live malloc'd array and simply refers to somebody else's connection. Recorded as system-malloc because that is where the bytes came from, but verdict blind, by the same reasoning the peer lane applied to ngx_slab: a free that never reaches the system allocator is not a free anything can see. The associated ngx_quic_connection_t is separately ngx_pcalloc'd from c->pool.

trigger: ngx_quic_free_buffer() returned the chain to the recycle lists and cleared qb->chain but left qb->last_chain pointing at a link that had already been recycled; any subsequent use of the ngx_quic_buffer_t would follow it.
poc: Hardening fix -- the maintainer states no reaching path was demonstrated ('While normally an ngx_quic_buffer_t object should not be used after freeing')
notes: Objects: the ngx_chain_t links and their ngx_buf_t headers, both pool-allocated (ngx_buf_t via ngx_palloc(c->pool, sizeof(ngx_buf_t)) at src/event/quic/ngx_event_quic_frames.c:56 and :139, chain links via ngx_quic_alloc_chain at :513) and recycled through qc->free_bufs (:37-40, :113-114) and the pool's own pool->chain free list (ngx_buf.c:48-65). The 4096-byte payloads (ngx_pnalloc(c->pool, NGX_QUIC_BUFFER_SIZE) at :67) are worth noting separately: NGX_QUIC_BUFFER_SIZE is 4096, ONE byte over pool->max=4095, so those go to ngx_palloc_large -> malloc; but they too are recycled via qc->free_bufs and never reach free(), so malloc never sees the reuse. Verdict blind on both halves. Non-CVE (a one-line defensive nulling); shipped in the 1.27.0 release that also carried the QUIC security batch, but this commit is not individually named in CHANGES so no CVE is asserted.

trigger: While closing streams, ngx_quic_close_streams() calls each stream's read event handler; that handler could recursively destroy the NEXT stream, which the loop had already saved a pointer to. In HTTP/3 the path is ngx_http_request_handler -> ngx_http_v3_send_cancel_stream failing on the decoder stream that happens to be next in tree order.
poc: HTTP/3 session where a request stream is cancelled and the decoder stream is the next stream in the QUIC stream tree, with the cancel-instruction send failing
notes: Object: ngx_quic_stream_t, allocated `qs = ngx_palloc(c->pool, sizeof(ngx_quic_stream_t))` at src/event/quic/ngx_event_quic_streams.c:679 -- carved from the QUIC connection's pool, so a bump allocation. The fix postpones calling read handlers until all streams have been collected. When the stream is destroyed the surrounding ngx_destroy_pool (src/event/quic/ngx_event_quic_streams.c:191) does release the stream's OWN 16K pool to malloc, but qs itself lives in the parent connection pool which stays alive, so the dangling pointer remains a valid in-bounds arena pointer. Non-CVE.

trigger: Handshake-level CRYPTO frames sent AFTER the client's Finished message, in the same packet as the Finished frame. The handshake keys are already discarded, so the send context and its crypto buffer are in a torn-down state; the commit states this 'could lead to memory disclosure and a potential segfault'.
poc: QUIC client that coalesces additional handshake-level CRYPTO frames into the packet carrying its Finished message
notes: Object: the ngx_quic_buffer_t crypto reassembly buffer of the handshake send context (ctx->crypto), whose chain links and ngx_buf_t headers are pool-allocated and free-listed (src/event/quic/ngx_event_quic_frames.c:56, :218, :513) and whose 4096-byte payloads are ngx_pnalloc(c->pool, NGX_QUIC_BUFFER_SIZE) at :67 -- 4096 is one byte over pool->max=4095 so those specific payloads take the large/malloc path, but are then recycled via qc->free_bufs (:37-40) and never freed. The fix guards on ngx_quic_keys_available(). The disclosed bytes are recycled arena content. Shipped in the 1.27.0 release that carried the QUIC security batch (CVE-2024-32760, CVE-2024-31079, CVE-2024-35200, CVE-2024-34161); CHANGES does not attribute individual commits, so NO CVE id is asserted for this row.

trigger: The cleanup handler calls ngx_quic_shutdown_stream() and then clears sc->connection. If the shutdown FAILED, sc->connection was left set while the application had already freed the connection, so a later close attempt freed it a second time.
poc: QUIC stream whose shutdown fails during cleanup (e.g. the connection is already in error), then closed again
notes: Object: the stream's ngx_connection_t, from the per-worker cycle->connections array (ngx_alloc at src/event/ngx_event.c:754-755) recycled via cycle->free_connections (ngx_connection.c:1229-1239 / :1279-1280). The commit calls it an 'allocator double free error', but the 'free' is ngx_free_connection pushing the slot back on nginx's own free list -- so the second free does not hit the system allocator's double-free detection; it simply puts the same slot on the list twice, after which two different sessions get the same ngx_connection_t. Verdict blind for that reason. The stream's 16K pool (ngx_create_pool(NGX_DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE, ...) at ngx_event_quic_streams.c:693) IS destroyed to malloc, so a glibc/hardened allocator would see a genuine double free only if the same pool were destroyed twice, which is not what happens here. Ticket #2586. Non-CVE.

trigger: With OpenSSL 3.5 the crypto_release_rcd QUIC callback can fire late, after the QUIC connection was already closed on handshake failure -- for instance when the client's Finished message does not align with a TLS record boundary.
poc: QUIC handshake failure with OpenSSL 3.5 where the client Finished message straddles a record boundary
notes: Object: ngx_quic_connection_t, ngx_pcalloc'd from the QUIC connection pool, reached via ngx_quic_get_connection(c) inside the callback. On a handshake failure the connection pool is destroyed, which does return its blocks to malloc (ngx_destroy_pool, ngx_palloc.c:89-95, calls ngx_free on both the large list and the block chain) -- so a quarantining allocator could in principle catch THIS one. It is still classified blind because the pointer that survives is an interior pointer at block+sizeof(ngx_pool_t) (80 bytes in, measured) rather than a chunk base, and because every OTHER object that shared the block is indistinguishable from it. Non-CVE.

trigger: A cached PTR response where ngx_resolver_dup() fails to allocate memory for the resulting name. The original resolver node was freed but left in expire_queue, so a later address resolution walked the queue into freed memory.
poc: PTR resolution under memory pressure so that ngx_resolver_dup() returns NULL for a cached entry, followed by another address resolution
notes: CONTROL GROUP. Object: ngx_resolver_node_t (sizeof measured 184 bytes), allocated `ngx_resolver_alloc(r, sizeof(ngx_resolver_node_t))` at src/core/ngx_resolver.c:810 and :1044. ngx_resolver_alloc is a thin wrapper over ngx_alloc (= malloc) at src/core/ngx_resolver.c:4161, and ngx_resolver_free is a real ngx_free (= free) at :4189 -- independently confirmed against the source and cross-checked with the peer lane. So the whole resolver subsystem sits outside the pool: every node is an individually malloc'd, individually freed chunk, and this dangling expire_queue entry is exactly what a quarantining or CHERI-style allocator revokes. The fix is to leave the node intact rather than to free it. Same defect class as several of the pool rows above; the only difference is the allocator, which is the comparison this survey exists to make. Non-CVE.

trigger: A DNS response whose final byte is the first octet of a compression pointer. The 0xc0 test consumed the second octet without checking p against 'last', so one byte past the end of the response was read and used as part of the pointer offset.
poc: Crafted DNS response truncated so that a compression pointer's high byte is the last byte of the message
notes: CONTROL GROUP, with an important caveat. The over-read source is the DNS response buffer. On the UDP path that buffer is a STACK array, `u_char buf[NGX_RESOLVER_UDP_SIZE]` at src/core/ngx_resolver.c:1584 -- no allocator involved at all. On the TCP path it is heap: `b->start = ngx_resolver_alloc(r, NGX_RESOLVER_TCP_RSIZE)` at :1376, i.e. malloc via ngx_resolver_alloc (:4161), which is where the 'caught' verdict applies. The maintainer judged it harmless ('in the worst case it uses some uninitialized memory as a part of the compression pointer length'). Recorded because the same defect recurred: see nginx-resolver-copy-off-by-one-srv. Non-CVE.

trigger: An SRV response where the record's data begins exactly at the end of the message: the bounds test was `i + 6 > n` where it needed `i + 6 >= n`, so ngx_resolver_copy() was handed a source pointer one byte past the response.
poc: Crafted SRV DNS response truncated so that the name field starts exactly at the message end
notes: CONTROL GROUP. Same object and same caveat as the 2021 row: UDP responses are read into the stack array at src/core/ngx_resolver.c:1584, TCP responses into ngx_resolver_alloc(r, NGX_RESOLVER_TCP_RSIZE) at :1376 (malloc, per ngx_resolver_alloc at :4161). The commit says explicitly 'It is believed to be harmless, see a similar change 077a890a76ff' -- i.e. the maintainers themselves link it to the 2021 fix. Recording both is the point: the identical off-by-one in the identical function five years apart, in the one nginx subsystem that does NOT use the pool. Non-CVE.

trigger: When validating the second or a later certificate in a chain, the SSL callback could be invoked twice to report the same error. The first invocation terminates the client connection and releases its memory; the second reads and writes that released memory. Reachable via failure to create the OCSP request, to start resolving the responder name, or to start connecting to it.
poc: ssl_ocsp on; with a certificate chain of 2+ certificates where OCSP request creation or responder resolution fails
notes: Object: ngx_ssl_ocsp_ctx_t (sizeof measured 456 bytes) allocated `ngx_pcalloc(pool, sizeof(ngx_ssl_ocsp_ctx_t))` at src/event/ngx_event_openssl_stapling.c:1312, out of a DEDICATED 2048-byte pool created one line earlier at :1307. For a 2048-byte pool, pool->max = 2048 - sizeof(ngx_pool_t) = 1968 (computed from the measured sizeof(ngx_pool_t)=80), so the 456-byte ctx is comfortably a bump carve, as are its siblings (the ngx_log_t at :1318, the addrs at :1500, the base64 request at :1791). The client connection's own pool is what gets destroyed. Blind: the ctx and every sibling live in one 2048-byte block with no internal boundaries, so a stale ctx pointer is indistinguishable from a stale pointer to any of them. Non-CVE.
